items.title: Morning Briefing: Oct. 31, 2026
items.excerpt: 31 October 2026• Update: 31 October 2026 Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Saturday, including Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborting an Africa trip and returning to Warsaw as a power struggle erupts over control of the Constitutional Tribunal; Türkiye formally nominating OSCE Secretary-General Feridun Sinirlioglu as a candidate for UN secretary-general; and the US State Department approving a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE missiles to Ukraine. Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborted a flight to Senegal and returned to Warsaw as rival groups of judges disputed control of the Constitutional Tribunal, after orders appeared on its website to temporarily remove its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president Bartlomiej Sochanski, in a move the tribunal rejected as illegal and a "coup." Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska said she ordered the two to stop their duties, while police said they were deployed for possible threats to judges and had not entered the building. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said "restoring the rule of law is our duty," while opposition Law and Justice leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski called the events a "coup against the Constitutional Tribunal." Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski defended the police action as aimed at letting duly elected judges resume the court’s work, while US Ambassador Tom Rose urged restraint, calling the situation "very serious." ## Türkiye nominates OSCE chief Sinirlioglu as candidate for next UN secretary-general Türkiye formally nominated Feridun Sinirlioglu, secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, as a candidate for UN secretary-general, after the latest Security Council straw poll ended inconclusively, according to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources. In a nomination letter transmitted by Türkiye's UN envoy Ahmet Yildiz to the presidents of the General Assembly and the Security Council, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan cited Sinirlioglu's more than 40 years in diplomacy, including as foreign minister and UN envoy, saying he possesses "the experience and culture of consensus required to lead the United Nations Organization." ## US approves $2.1B Patriot missile sale to Ukraine The US State Department approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement missiles and related equipment to Ukraine at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion, saying the cost is "funded entirely by partners and allies" and that "no US funds are involved in this sale." Ukraine will pay with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, according to the agency, with Lockheed Martin as principal contractor. The approval comes days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors per month from the US this year, while needing to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month. ... - Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez acknowledged that "trust in high-speed rail has been shattered" after a collision near Urda killed at least 69 people earlier this week, the country's second major high-speed rail disaster this year.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: Published ... The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. ... September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%.

items.title: Election 2026 live updates: Judge orders Trump administration to stop intimidating election officials
items.excerpt: ## Federal judge warns Trump administration's efforts to intervene in election could deter voters A federal judge in Washington warned this afternoon that the Trump administration’s efforts to intervene in elections could have a “chilling effect,” noting that letters the Justice Department has sent to local election officials have included inaccurate data. “The government has made no secret of their determination to purge the voter rolls” of individuals they believe to be noncitizens, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said during a rare Saturday hearing. “Past efforts to do so have resulted in U.S. citizens being swept up into this law enforcement dragnet.” Chutkan said she was concerned people may not go to the polls if they’re afraid they could be wrongly accused of noncitizen voting. “It’s an ‘if,’” Elizabeth Shapiro, an attorney for the Justice Department, shot back. “It’s not,” Chutkan said, citing Gustavo Gutierrez Gomez, who filed a declaration in the case, brought by voting advocates over what they call the Trump administration’s “Voter Data Collection Policy.” The League of United Latin American Citizens, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, asked the judge to block the transmission of data about registered voters the administration claims are “likely noncitizens” to states and localities for the purpose of taking special action with those voters. At today's hearing, Chutkan pointed to several cases in Washington, D.C., and around the country where voting groups or immigrant rights groups are asking for similar relief, noting that Trump administration doesn’t have a stellar track record of identifying actual noncitizen voters. “The government’s been wrong,” Chutkan said. “In fact, they’ve very rarely been right.” The judge noted the DOJ’s efforts in Nevada to alert local election officials of 15,903 people it argued were noncitizen voters. There, officials ultimately confirmed that no one on the list was a noncitizen. “I cannot disagree with you the government has made mistakes,” Shapiro said. “The government is not trying to make mistakes.”

items.excerpt: Oct. 30, 2026, 10:19 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 31, 2026, 7:06 PM EDT By Gary Grumbach and Kyla Guilfoil The Trump administration on Saturday appealed a sweeping order handed down by a federal judge the day prior to block the administration from threatening or intimidating election officials in the weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The motion to appeal the order was filed by the Justice Department to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in California. It seeks to overturn an eight-page order issued Friday that prohibits any action that may “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote.” “In the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election,” wrote U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson, who is based in California. The order comes in the wake of efforts to require states like California and Washington to separate out ballots the administration says could be cast by noncitizens. An appeals court ruled against the administration in California this week; the Washington case is pending. “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” Thompson wrote Friday. items.excerpt: - AP - Oct 31, 2026 - Oct 31, 2026 Updated 14 hrs ago Houdini’s centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Houdini, a century after his death, continues to captivate. A rare essay by the escape artist has been published, shedding light on his early influences. A recent book revisits questions about the cause and date of his death. Houdini, born Erik Weisz, became an international celebrity known for his escape acts. His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated, with new theories challenging the official cause. Centennial events this weekend include a "Grand Houdini Centenarium" in Budapest, an auction in Hollywood, and seances in Chicago and Maryland. Despite the intrigue, experts say his legacy endures through his remarkable life. Scott Clifton and Tamara Tunie earn lead acting Daytime Emmys. 'General Hospital' wins again LOS ANGELES (AP) — Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” have won lead acting honors at the Daytime Emmy Awards. It's Clifton's second career trophy in the lead category. Tunie made her return to the soap opera genre after 17 years away. “General Hospital” won its record 19th trophy overall as outstanding drama and sixth in a row. Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category for her former Netflix show “With Love, Meghan.” Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. An introspective Kirk Franklin is no longer apologizing with 'I Am What I Am' album NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart. Known for his crossover hits, the 20-time Grammy winner has frequently faced criticism for working with secular artists, but remains unapologetic in the name of spreading his Christian faith. 'Time is the fire in which we burn': 2 major cast losses rock the passionate 'Star Trek' universe WASHINGTON (AP) — First Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original series during the 1960s, died at age 90. Then, three days later, the cosmos lost Patrick Stewart. The Shakespearean actor in 1987 became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, the unlikely and poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have made the present sting. William Shatner played Capt. James T. Kirk in the original series in the 1960s. He called it a “heartbreaking week.” ... Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence. Ross has pleaded not guilty to all charges. Officials say Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police. Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86 Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a “Star Trek” franchise and the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86. A spokesperson said Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia. Stewart was best known as Professor Charles Xavier from the “X-Men” and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” but he spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
